Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a finite integer
maximum $K\ge1$, prescheduled information fractions
$0<t_1<\cdots<t_K=1$ (where $t_j$ is the fraction of total planned
information available at look $j$), and a nominal level $\alpha\in(0,1)$. An
**alpha-spending function** is a nondecreasing map
$A:[0,1]\to[0,\alpha]$ with $A(0)=0$ and $A(1)=\alpha$.

Under the stipulated simple null law $P_0$, the standardized look vector is
$Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K)\sim N_K(0,\Sigma)$, where
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\sqrt{t_j/t_k}\quad(j\le k),\qquad \Sigma_{jk}=\Sigma_{kj}\quad(j>k).$$
Here $N_K$ is the finite-dimensional multivariate normal law of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], whose projection characterization determines
the law by [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]].
The construction of this covariance matrix as a valid Gaussian covariance is
proved in [[thm-group-sequential-alpha-spending-calibration]]. The standardized
coordinates are correlated; independence of the $Z_j$ is not assumed.

For a **one-sided upper-boundary design**, look $j$ rejects when
$Z_j\ge b_j$. For a **symmetric two-sided design**, look $j$ rejects when
$|Z_j|\ge c_j$. In either case, the procedure stops at its first crossing.
For each $k$, its cumulative type-I probability is the probability under the
stipulated null law of crossing at one of looks $1,\ldots,k$. The design is
exactly calibrated to $A$ when this cumulative probability equals $A(t_k)$
for every $k$. If it is embedded in an experiment with a nonempty alternative
and singleton null hypothesis, this null rejection probability is the test
size in the sense of [[def-test-size-and-power]].

The fractions and joint null law are assumptions of this definition. It does
not derive a Gaussian model from an asymptotic central limit theorem, justify
data-dependent look timing, justify estimated variance, or establish error
control over an unspecified composite null. A two-sided design calibrates its
two-sided crossing events separately; one-sided boundaries are not doubled
to obtain two-sided boundaries.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

**Inputs:** The Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and a canonical design from
[[def-group-sequential-alpha-spending-design]] and a mode, either one-sided
upper-boundary or symmetric two-sided.

**Output:** The look boundaries for the selected mode.

Set $t_0=0$, $R_0=\varnothing$, and process $k=1,\ldots,K$ in order. Let
$R_{k-1}$ be the union of the crossing events already defined at the earlier
looks.

- If $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$, set the boundary at look $k$ to $+\infty$. Its
  crossing event is empty, so $R_k=R_{k-1}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is one-sided, choose the real number
  $b_k$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is symmetric two-sided, choose
  $c_k\ge0$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\}$.

The root-existence theorem
[[thm-group-sequential-alpha-spending-calibration]] proves that every
positive spending increment has a unique finite solution; the algorithm
therefore makes no arbitrary boundary selection. The procedure specifies
exact boundaries under the supplied joint null law. It does not prescribe a
numerical integration package or tolerance.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $1\le i\le j\le K$, define a lower-triangular matrix $L$ by $L_{j1}=\sqrt{t_1/t_j}$ and, for $2\le i\le j$, $L_{ji}=\sqrt{(t_i-t_{i-1})/t_j}$, with $L_{ji}=0$ for $i>j$. For $j\le k$, the $(j,k)$ entry of $LL^T$ is $$\frac{t_1+\sum_{i=2}^{j}(t_i-t_{i-1})}{\sqrt{t_jt_k}}=\sqrt{t_j/t_k}=\Sigma_{jk}.$$ Thus $\Sigma=LL^T$. Its diagonal entries in $L$ are $1$ and $\sqrt{(t_i-t_{i-1})/t_i}>0$ for $i\ge2$, so $L$ is invertible and $v^T\Sigma v=\|L^Tv\|^2>0$ for every nonzero $v$.

For every $k$, the $k$th coordinate has law $N(0,1)$ by the projection clause in [F2]. It has no atoms, and for $x<y$, $$0<P_0(x<Z_k<y)=\int_x^y\phi(u)\,du\le\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$$ Positivity follows from [F5]; the upper bound follows from $0<e^{-u^2/2}\le1$. The same facts bound a two-sided strip by $P_0(c<|Z_k|<d)\le2(d-c)/\sqrt{2\pi}$ when $0\le c<d$.

By [F2] and [F3], the canonical law exists and is represented by $Z=\Sigma^{1/2}Y$ for independent standard-normal coordinates $Y$. Since $\Sigma$ is positive definite by step 1.1, $\Sigma^{1/2}$ is invertible: if $\Sigma^{1/2}v=0$, then $v^T\Sigma v=0$, forcing $v=0$. The inverse image under this linear homeomorphism of any nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^K$ is nonempty and open, hence contains a product of nonempty open intervals. Each interval has positive standard-normal probability by [F4]–[F5], and independence makes the product probability positive. Therefore every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^K$ has positive $P_0$-probability.

For the induction step, fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. Assume that the boundaries through $k-1$ have been constructed with $P_0(R_{k-1})=A(t_{k-1})$; for $k=1$ this is the empty base case $R_0=\varnothing$, $A(t_0)=A(0)=0$. Any finite two-sided boundary already constructed is positive, as established when its root was obtained. Let $S=R_{k-1}^c$. In the one-sided mode, $S$ is the intersection of the open conditions $Z_j<b_j$ for earlier finite boundaries; in the symmetric two-sided mode, it is the intersection of $|Z_j|<c_j$ for earlier finite boundaries. These conditions describe a nonempty open set: choose each constrained coordinate below its upper boundary, or inside its interval $(-c_j,c_j)$, and ignore infinite boundaries. Thus $P_0(S)=1-A(t_{k-1})\ge1-\alpha>0$.

In the one-sided mode set $q(x)=A(t_{k-1})+P_0(S\cap\{Z_k\ge x\})$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. If $x<y$, then $q(x)-q(y)=P_0(S\cap\{x\le Z_k<y\})>0$. Although $S\subseteq\mathbb R^K$, it restricts only coordinates $j<k$, as described in step 3.1. Thus $O_{x,y}:=S\cap\{z\in\mathbb R^K:x<z_k<y\}$ is nonempty and open: choose each earlier coordinate below its finite one-sided boundary (or arbitrarily when its boundary is $+\infty$), choose $z_k\in(x,y)$, and choose the remaining coordinates arbitrarily. By step 2.1, $P_0(O_{x,y})>0$; the only part of $S\cap\{x\le Z_k<y\}$ omitted from $O_{x,y}$ lies on $Z_k=x$, which has probability zero by step 1.2. Also $|q(x)-q(y)|\le(y-x)/\sqrt{2\pi}$ by step 1.2, so $q$ is continuous. Moreover $q(x)\to1$ as $x\to-\infty$ and $q(x)\to A(t_{k-1})$ as $x\to+\infty$, since the omitted lower and upper normal tails tend to zero. For the symmetric two-sided mode set $q(c)=A(t_{k-1})+P_0(S\cap\{|Z_k|\ge c\})$ for $c\ge0$. For $0\le c<d$, $q(c)-q(d)=P_0(S\cap\{c\le|Z_k|<d\})>0$. Here $S$ again restricts only coordinates $j<k$, so $O_{c,d}:=S\cap\{z\in\mathbb R^K:c<|z_k|<d\}$ is nonempty and open: set every earlier coordinate to $0$ (which satisfies every finite earlier symmetric no-crossing condition because its boundary is positive), choose $z_k=(c+d)/2$, and choose the remaining coordinates arbitrarily. Step 2.1 gives $P_0(O_{c,d})>0$. The bound in step 1.2 makes $q$ continuous. Here $q(0)=1$ and $q(c)\to A(t_{k-1})$ as $c\to+\infty$. The tail limits in both modes follow from [F6] applied to increasing lower or central intervals of the standard-normal coordinate.

Since $A$ is nondecreasing, either $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$ or $A(t_{k-1})<A(t_k)\le\alpha<1$. In the flat case, [F9] assigns $+\infty$, whose crossing event is empty, so the previous cumulative probability is unchanged. In the increasing case, the target lies strictly between the endpoint limits of $q$. The limits in step 3.2 give finite endpoints on which the continuous function takes values on opposite sides of $A(t_k)$; [F7] gives a root. Strict decrease in step 3.2 makes that finite root unique. The induction therefore defines every boundary through the finite maximum $K$. In the symmetric two-sided mode $q(0)=1>A(t_k)$, so the root is strictly positive.

The induction step is complete: at an increasing look the selected root gives $P_0(R_k)=A(t_k)$ by [F9]; at a flat look the event union is unchanged and $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$. Induction from $R_0=\varnothing$ proves the equality for every $k$. Stopping at the first crossing makes $R_k$ exactly the event of rejection by look $k$. At $k=K$, $t_K=1$ and $A(1)=\alpha$, so the terminal simple-null rejection probability is $\alpha$. For any embedding with a nonempty alternative and singleton null $\{\theta_0\}$ whose law is $P_0$, the rejection indicator is a measurable test function because $R_K$ is a finite union of Borel threshold events; [F8] then makes its size $\alpha$. AC is used in the supplied Gaussian law and representation [F2] and [F4], not in the finite root selection: each root is unique and there are only finitely many looks.

boundaries.reason: K is a positive finite integer, so the induction has a nonempty finite index set.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 4.1 and 5.1 treat a flat increment; its +infinity crossing event is empty and cumulative spend is unchanged.
Step 5.1 uses t_K=1 and A(1)=alpha to obtain the terminal null rejection probability.
Steps 1.1–2.1 prove positive-definite covariance and full support; step 3.1 covers the K=1 induction base case.
Steps 3.2 and 5.1 use the boundary-function tails and final endpoint t_K=1.
Facts A1, F2 and F4 state the AC branch for Gaussian suppliers; step 5.1 notes no additional choice in the unique finite recursion.

Assume AC and the canonical group-sequential design of
[[def-group-sequential-alpha-spending-design]]. The recursive boundary
algorithm [[alg-group-sequential-alpha-spending-boundary-calibration]] is

Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Since $\exp(0)=1$ by its power series and $\exp$ is strictly increasing by [F9], $e=\exp(1)>1$. Thus $1+(e-1)t$ increases from $1$ to $e$ as $t$ goes from $0$ to $1$. By [F7]–[F8], $A_P(0)=0$, $A_P(1)=\alpha\log e=\alpha$, and $A_P$ is nondecreasing with values in $[0,\alpha]$. At $t_1=1/2$ this gives $a_1=\alpha\log((1+e)/2)$ and $0<a_1<\alpha$.

The standard normal CDF satisfies $\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)=\int_x^y\phi(s)\,ds$ for $x<y$. By [F4]–[F5], this difference is positive and at most $(y-x)/\sqrt{2\pi}$, so $\Phi$ is strictly increasing and continuous. Its limits at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$ are $0$ and $1$: [F10] applied to $(-n,\infty)$ gives the lower-tail limit, and [F10] applied to $(-\infty,n]$ gives the upper-tail limit; the density has no point masses. Therefore [F11] gives a unique $q(u)$ for every $u\in(0,1)$. In particular $c_1=q(1-a_1/2)$ is finite, positive, and symmetry and atomlessness give $P_0(|Z_1|\ge c_1)=a_1$.

The canonical covariance matrix is $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/\sqrt2\\1/\sqrt2&1\end{pmatrix}$, so its determinant is $1/2>0$ and the correlation is $1/\sqrt2$. Applying [F2]–[F3] at the second look gives the unique finite $c_2$ satisfying the displayed cumulative two-sided crossing equation. The event $\{|Z_1|\ge c_1\}$ and the continued-path event $\{|Z_1|<c_1,\ |Z_2|\ge c_2\}$ are disjoint and their union is the final rejection event. Hence the continued-path event has joint probability $\alpha-a_1$, and since $P_0(|Z_1|<c_1)=1-a_1>0$, its conditional probability given continuation is $(\alpha-a_1)/(1-a_1)$. The total rejection probability is $A_P(1)=\alpha$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a finite integer
maximum $K\ge1$, prescheduled information fractions
$0<t_1<\cdots<t_K=1$ (where $t_j$ is the fraction of total planned
information available at look $j$), and a nominal level $\alpha\in(0,1)$. An
**alpha-spending function** is a nondecreasing map
$A:[0,1]\to[0,\alpha]$ with $A(0)=0$ and $A(1)=\alpha$.

Under the stipulated simple null law $P_0$, the standardized look vector is
$Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K)\sim N_K(0,\Sigma)$, where
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\sqrt{t_j/t_k}\quad(j\le k),\qquad \Sigma_{jk}=\Sigma_{kj}\quad(j>k).$$
Here $N_K$ is the finite-dimensional multivariate normal law of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], whose projection characterization determines
the law by [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]].
The construction of this covariance matrix as a valid Gaussian covariance is
proved in [[thm-group-sequential-alpha-spending-calibration]]. The standardized
coordinates are correlated; independence of the $Z_j$ is not assumed.

For a **one-sided upper-boundary design**, look $j$ rejects when
$Z_j\ge b_j$. For a **symmetric two-sided design**, look $j$ rejects when
$|Z_j|\ge c_j$. In either case, the procedure stops at its first crossing.
For each $k$, its cumulative type-I probability is the probability under the
stipulated null law of crossing at one of looks $1,\ldots,k$. The design is
exactly calibrated to $A$ when this cumulative probability equals $A(t_k)$
for every $k$. If it is embedded in an experiment with a nonempty alternative
and singleton null hypothesis, this null rejection probability is the test
size in the sense of [[def-test-size-and-power]].

The fractions and joint null law are assumptions of this definition. It does
not derive a Gaussian model from an asymptotic central limit theorem, justify
data-dependent look timing, justify estimated variance, or establish error
control over an unspecified composite null. A two-sided design calibrates its
two-sided crossing events separately; one-sided boundaries are not doubled
to obtain two-sided boundaries.

**Inputs:** The Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and a canonical design from
[[def-group-sequential-alpha-spending-design]] and a mode, either one-sided
upper-boundary or symmetric two-sided.

**Output:** The look boundaries for the selected mode.

Set $t_0=0$, $R_0=\varnothing$, and process $k=1,\ldots,K$ in order. Let
$R_{k-1}$ be the union of the crossing events already defined at the earlier
looks.

- If $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$, set the boundary at look $k$ to $+\infty$. Its
  crossing event is empty, so $R_k=R_{k-1}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is one-sided, choose the real number
  $b_k$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is symmetric two-sided, choose
  $c_k\ge0$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\}$.

The root-existence theorem
[[thm-group-sequential-alpha-spending-calibration]] proves that every
positive spending increment has a unique finite solution; the algorithm
therefore makes no arbitrary boundary selection. The procedure specifies
exact boundaries under the supplied joint null law. It does not prescribe a
numerical integration package or tolerance.

Assume AC and the canonical group-sequential design of
[[def-group-sequential-alpha-spending-design]]. The recursive boundary
algorithm [[alg-group-sequential-alpha-spending-boundary-calibration]] is
well-defined: every positive spending increment has a unique finite boundary,
while a zero increment has boundary $+\infty$. For every $k$, the probability
under $P_0$ of a rejection by look $k$ is $A(t_k)$; in particular the terminal
simple-null rejection probability is $\alpha$. When embedded in an experiment
with a nonempty alternative and a singleton null whose law is $P_0$, the test
size is therefore $\alpha$. The same cumulative-probability conclusion holds
for separately calibrated symmetric two-sided crossing events. This exact
statement is conditional on the specified joint Gaussian null law and
prescheduled information fractions; it does not cover data-dependent timing,
an estimated variance, or a composite null without an additional argument.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
